handover19.text: Morning, {called}. Three months a surgeon, and today's the first list with only your name on it. No 'under Dr. Iyer'. Just you.
Post from Margao. Mrs. Gomes at the wedding, in the blue sari, with a walking frame covered in marigolds. On the back: 'NO WHISPERING'.

then.text: Zoya's on Dr. Bhatt's team now. She asked to move. She didn't say why. She didn't have to.
then.head: down

else.text: Zoya's on Dr. Bhatt's team this month. She rang twice yesterday to tell you she'd caught a warfarin.

handover19.text: Now. Your team. Tom's on the board, but he did a double: the night list, then a burns case until six.
I'm fine. Two coffees and a samosa. That's basically sleep.
Or Neha Joshi. New, from the heart theatres in Pune. Counts like a bank cashier. She's in the corridor, pretending not to listen.

choose.text: Tom, go home and sleep. Neha scrubs with me today.

then.text: ...Thank you. Honestly. I'd have counted my own fingers wrong.
then.head: nod

then.text: Neha! You're scrubbing. Stop pretending you didn't hear.

choose.text: Tom. We've done fifty operations together. I want hands I know.

then.text: Fifty-one, after today. I'll count twice.
then.head: nod

then.text: Count three times, Tom.

handover19.text: Gas. Dr. Khan's on the eye list until half past eleven. Dr. Arindam Bose is free now. Quick, good hands, famous for reading the notes in the lift.

choose.text: Dr. Bose. She's been vomiting for two days. I don't want her waiting.

then.text: Then you tell him everything about her. He won't ask.

choose.text: Dr. Khan. I'd rather wait two hours for someone who reads everything.

then.text: Two more hours of a twisted bowel. Your call. That's what the job is now.

handover19.text: Your name's on the board outside Theatre 2. In capitals. Mr. Malhotra had it laminated.
Priya: Admissions. Sixty-four, vomiting since Saturday, belly like a drum. She wants a doctor with a strong stomach.

kurup_arrive.text: Mrs. Shanta Kurup, sixty-four. Vomiting since Saturday night. Her belly's tight as a drum, and nothing's come out the other end since Friday.
Venu Kurup. Husband. Forty-one years. I parked in the ambulance bay. It felt like an emergency.

choose.text: Mrs. Kurup, I'm {called}. Questions first, then I'll examine you. Venu can stay.

then.text: He stays. He's useless, but he stays.
Forty-one years of useless.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Priya: drip, a tube to empty her stomach, bloods. I'll ask the questions while you work.

then.text: Drip's in. Tube's ready. She's going to hate the tube.
then.head: nod

then.text: I already hate the tube. I haven't met it yet.

kurup_arrive.text: Ask her everything theatre will need, Doctor. Quickly. She's going grey.

then.text: An open gallbladder, here, in 2004. I've asked Records for her old notes. They'll come up from the basement by tonight, if the lift works.

else.text: There's an old scar down her belly, Doctor. Nobody's asked her about it yet.

then.text: Asthma, two inhalers. The anaesthetist needs to hear that before she's asleep.
Tell Dr. Bose yourself. Twice. He reads notes the way I read horoscopes.
Plaster allergy. Paper tape on everything. I'll put a sign over her bed.
then.head: nod

kurup_after.text: So. You'll cut me open. Again. The last one left me a scar like a railway line.

choose.text: Your bowel is blocked, probably by scar from the old operation. I'll open your belly and free it. If a piece is damaged, I may take it out and join the ends.

then.text: Take a piece out. How long a piece?
then.head: tilt

then.text: As little as I can. Maybe none.
Then none, please. I'm attached to it.

choose.text: It's routine. Sign here, and you'll be sorted by lunch.

then.text: Routine. That's what they said in 2004.
Sign it, Venu. I'm too sick to argue, which is a first.

kurup_after.text: Doctor. I know it's your job. Be careful anyway.

then.title: Two hours later
then.text: Mrs. Kurup was sick twice more. Dr. Khan came up from the eye list with every page of her notes read.

kurup_ready.text: Venu, if I don't wake up, the gas bill is in the biscuit tin.
You'll wake up. I can't even find the biscuit tin.
Doctor. The last surgeon had a very serious moustache and very cold hands. Warm your hands.
kurup_ready.head: tilt

obstruction_brief.text: Your list, {called}. Your patient, your cut. I'm assisting. Pretend I'm furniture. Furniture with opinions.

then.text: Neha Joshi. Swabs in tens, instruments in eights, and everything goes on the board as it goes in. Including the cotton.

else.text: Count's ready. I'll do it twice. Third coffee's working.
else.head: nod

then.text: Arindam Bose. Gas. Sixty-four, blocked bowel. Anything I should know? I read the front page in the lift.
Asthma. Two inhalers, and stairs make her wheeze.
Ah. Then her inhaler goes down the tube, and I go gently. Lovely. Somebody reads.
then.head: nod

else.text: Nothing I know of.
Then nothing it is. Quick sleep, quick start.
Sorry for the wait. I listened to her chest: she wheezes like a harmonium. Inhaler first, then sleep. And two more hours of vomiting won't have made her bowel happier.

then.text: Time-out, Doctor. I'll read the board.

else.text: Time-out, Doctor. I'll read the board.

then.text: She's whole and the bowel's free. I finished it. First list, the hardest kind of belly. Don't carry it. Learn it.
Clean. Your first list, and nobody watching would have guessed.
then.head: nod

else.text: Untidy in places. But she's whole, and the bowel's free.

then.text: A piece out and the ends joined. Watch her from day three to five. You remember Mr. Nanda.
The thin patch is stitched over. It'll hold.
then.head: nod

then.text: Dr. Bose asks me to pass on: next time, tell him about the asthma before she wheezes, not after. He's not wrong. Nobody asked her.

else.text: Her chest tightened under the gas. Dr. Khan was ready for it. She'd listened first.

then.text: And Tom lost a swab in the count. Found under the liver. He's gone home to sleep. Twenty-two years after somebody else didn't find one.
then.head: down

kurup_after_op.text: Cotton, from 2004, wrapped in scar. Records sent her old notes up. Open gallbladder, twelfth of March. Swab count: 'correct'. Signed by the registrar.
What was in her, Doctor? What's in the pot?

choose.text: An old surgical swab, left from her first operation. It caused the blockage. I'm sorry. We'll explain it all to her when she wakes.

then.text: Twenty-two years. She's had tummy aches for twenty-two years. We blamed my cooking.
Thank you, {called}. Most people take a week to find those words.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Something from her first operation. When she's awake, I'll explain everything to you both, with her notes in my hand.

then.text: Tomorrow. I've apparently waited twenty-two years. I can wait a night.
then.head: nod

then.text: Tomorrow, {called}. Not the day after. And not 'adhesions'.

morning20.text: I read her notes again at midnight. The nurse in 2004 wrote 'count interrupted: emergency in casualty'. The registrar signed it correct anyway. At two in the morning.
Anand Rao was a good registrar. Exhausted, like all of them. That isn't a defence. It's a fact.
morning20.head: down

morning20.text: He's in his office with the door shut. He hasn't shut that door since his wife's operation.
He'll come to you. She's your patient now. Whatever he asks, remember who's in bed two.

choose.text: She's the first person I think about. Then him.

then.text: Good order.
then.head: nod

choose.text: He's my head of department. I'll hear him out.

then.text: Hear him out. Then decide like a surgeon, not a junior.

morning20.text: Dr. Rao: Could you come to the desk? Before you see Mrs. Kurup. Please.

rao_swab.text: Twelfth of March, 2004. A gallbladder at midnight, and a boy stabbed in casualty at one. They called me out with her belly open. I came back, closed, and signed what the nurse had started. 'Correct'.
rao_swab.head: down

rao_swab.text: I've told two hundred students: never sign a count you didn't finish. I was teaching them my own mistake, and I'd forgotten I made it.

then.text: Venu Kurup already knows. You told him last night. Good. That decides the easy part.
then.head: nod

then.text: I'd like to tell her the rest myself. With you beside me, or without you. Which?

choose.text: Together. Your mistake, my patient. We stand at her bed side by side.

then.text: Side by side. Yes. I'd have said the same to you, twenty years ago. Today I needed someone to say it to me.
then.head: nod

choose.text: It's yours to tell. I'll write exactly what I found, and answer anything she asks me.

then.text: Mine to tell. I'll go before the tea round, while I still have the nerve.
then.head: nod

else.text: The scan says 'adhesions'. Scar tissue. It's true, as far as it goes. The pot goes to the lab as 'foreign body', and nobody upstairs reads lab reports.
I'm two years from my pension. I'm asking, not ordering. What will you write?

choose.text: The truth. We tell her today, together. Your mistake, my patient, side by side at her bed.

then.text: ...Yes. Of course. I'd have said the same to you, twenty years ago. Today I needed someone to say it to me.
then.head: nod

choose.text: The truth. It's yours to tell her, and I'll write exactly what I found.

then.text: Mine to tell. I'll go before the tea round, while I still have the nerve.
then.head: nod

choose.text: I'll write adhesions. It's true, and it changes nothing for her now.

then.text: ...Thank you.
then.head: down

then.text: I thought I'd feel better.
Mrs. Kurup. I'm Anand Rao. In 2004 I operated on you. I left a swab inside you, and I wrote that the count was right. It wasn't. I am so sorry.
then.head: down

then.text: ...The moustache.
It went grey. So did I.
then.head: nod

then.text: Twenty-two years of tummy aches. And Venu's cooking blamed for every one of them.
I'd like an apology for the cooking, too.
You have it. Completely.
then.head: nod

then.text: You came and said it to my face. In 2004 nobody said anything to my face.
then.head: tilt

then.text: Dr. Rao came at seven, before the tea. Stood at the end of my bed like a schoolboy outside the headmaster's office. Told me everything.
He cried, a bit. I didn't. I'm saving it for the lawyer.
She's joking. Mostly.

else.text: So. What was it? The nurse in recovery said 'they found something'. Then she went pink and stopped talking.
else.head: tilt

choose.text: It was a swab, left from your first operation in 2004. It caused the blockage. I'm sorry. I should have said so this morning.

then.text: You nearly didn't tell me. I saw it on your face.
But you did.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Adhesions. Scar tissue from the old operation, wrapped round the bowel.

then.text: Scar tissue. Hm. In a pot. With a label.
then.head: tilt

then.text: Let it go, Shanta.
I was a postmistress for thirty years, Venu. I know when an envelope's been steamed.

choose.text: What happens now: we check your wound every day, you eat when your bowel wakes up, and the hospital writes to you formally. What happened, and why.

then.text: Formally. Good. I like things in writing. I was a postmistress.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Say nothing. Let her be angry for as long as she needs.

then.text: ...Thank you for not filling the silence. Doctors always fill the silence.
then.head: nod

kurup_truth.text: Promise me one thing. Whatever you change in that theatre, change it so this doesn't happen to the next Shanta.

choose.text: I'll put it to the department: nobody signs a count 'correct' unless they finished it themselves.

then.text: In writing.
In writing.

choose.text: I can't promise it'll never happen again. I can promise we'll count better.

then.text: Fair. I'd have known if you were lying, anyway.

morning21.text: News from the top floor, and it isn't about parking. Dr. Rao's called a meeting at four. Everyone. Even me. He's never asked for me.

then.text: And Mrs. Kurup's friends from the post office have heard. They've sent the ward a cake. It says 'HONEST' on it. In icing.

else.text: And Pathology rang. The pot from bed two: 'retained surgical swab, cotton'. They asked why the notes say 'adhesions'. I said you'd ring them.

morning21.text: Priya: Bed two. Mrs. Kurup has news. She's very proud of it. You'll want to sit down.

kurup_wind.text: Day two after a big belly operation, and her bowel has woken up.
A whisper, Doctor. This morning. Venu cheered. The man in bed one applauded.
Forty-one years married. I've never been so pleased by a noise.

then.text: Sips only today, for the join. Soup tomorrow if all's quiet.

else.text: Sips, then soup. Toast tomorrow, if she behaves.

then.text: And my promise?
then.head: tilt

then.text: Four o'clock. In front of everyone.

choose.text: Your bowel and I are both very relieved.

then.text: Put it in the notes. 'Bowel relieved. Surgeon also.'

choose.text: Wind means the bowel's moving again. Walk the corridor twice today. It helps.

then.text: Twice. I'll hold the drip.
then.head: nod

rao_retires.text: Thirty-one years in this building. I'll keep it short, which will be a first.
I'm retiring at the end of the month. Early. My wife is delighted. My golf is not.

then.text: Some of you have heard why. In 2004 I left a swab inside a patient and signed the count correct. This week a surgeon in this room found it, and made sure I told her. That is how this department should work. It's how it will work after me.
...Sir.
then.head: down

else.text: For personal reasons.
else.head: down

else.text: Personal reasons. Is that what we're calling it?

rao_retires.text: The board will appoint a new Head of Department. Interviews on Friday. Two internal candidates.
I've applied. A year and a half as a consultant, and I've done the management course. Twice.
And I've put your name forward, {called}. Don't look at me like that. I like operating. I don't like meetings. You can survive both.

then.text: Before we go. One change, whoever gets the job. Nobody signs a count 'correct' unless they finished it. If you're called away, the count starts again.
Seconded. It'll be on every theatre wall by Monday.

rao_retires.text: Friday, then. May the better surgeon win. Or the better talker. Malhotra's on the panel.

choose.text: Good luck, Kabir. I mean it.

then.text: Kabir. You've never called me that. ...Good luck.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Will you mention the parking space in your talk?

then.text: Only twice.

crash22.text: Doctor. Major incident. A city bus went off the flyover onto the market road. Forty on board. First ambulances in six minutes.
Dr. Iyer's in Theatre 1 with a burst aorta. Dr. Sethi's on his way in. Right now you're the senior surgeon on the floor.
The ambulance bay needs someone sorting them as they come off. Red in first, yellow waits, green walks. Black... somebody sits with black.

choose.text: Grace: everyone who can go home, send them now. We'll need every bed.

then.text: Six beds by ten. Mrs. Kurup offered to go home in a taxi. I said no.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Grace: ring everyone who's off duty. Nurses, residents, the lot.

then.text: Tom's on his way. Neha's already here. She says she never left.
then.head: nod

crash22.text: With me, Doctor. Bring the rules, not your feelings. Feelings are for later.
Priya: AMBULANCE BAY. NOW. The first ones are off.

triage_arrive.text: Walking wounded to the gate. Everyone else: you check, you tag, you move on. Thirty seconds each.
The loud ones will grab your sleeve. The quiet ones are the ones who die. Remember that.

then.text: Every tag right. Dr. Iyer's out of theatre, and she's walked the line. She didn't change a single one.
then.head: nod

then.text: Doctor. Someone you tagged to wait went grey in the corridor. Dr. Sethi took them into theatre forty minutes late.
The old man. He was bleeding inside, from his pelvis. He's alive. Just.
then.head: down

then.text: The quiet boy. A bleed on his brain. The neurosurgeons have him now.
then.head: down

choose.text: My tag. I'll go and see them.

then.text: Go. And next time, count the breaths, every time.
then.head: nod

choose.text: They looked fine when I saw them.

then.text: They always look fine. That's why there are rules.

else.text: Some tags were off, but nobody waited who couldn't. Dr. Iyer fixed the rest inside.

triage_after.text: Two died at the scene. Everyone who reached us alive is still alive. Go and drink some tea. Then the corridor.

crash_evening.text: Twenty-three admitted. Nine operations. One burst aorta who's going to be fine. And Priya sat with the black tags for an hour. Nobody told her to.
Six hours in theatre. Two spleens and a liver. I'm going to sleep in my car. In my parking space.

then.text: You ran the bay well. I'd say so even if we weren't both interviewing tomorrow.
then.head: nod

else.text: I hear the bay went... fine.

crash_evening.text: Doctors. The newspapers are downstairs. They want a photograph: the brave surgeons of the flyover. Both candidates. Smiling, ideally.

choose.text: No. Twenty-three people had the worst day of their lives. We're not smiling on top of it.

then.text: ...Fine. I'll tell them the surgeons are with patients. Which is, annoyingly, true.

choose.text: Photograph the nurses who ran the bay. Priya first.

then.text: Nurses. In the newspaper. The board will think I've gone soft.
You have.
then.head: nod

choose.text: One photo. It's good for the hospital.

then.text: I'll stand on the left. It's my better side.

crash_evening.text: Go home, {called}. Sleep. Tomorrow they'll ask what kind of head you'd be. You showed them today.
crash_evening.head: nod

morning23.text: Interview day. You look like you slept two hours. That's one more than Dr. Sethi.

then.text: Mrs. Kurup goes home today. She left you this: a letter for the board, sealed. You're to hand it over, and you're not allowed to read it.

else.text: Mrs. Kurup goes home today. With a copy of her pathology report. She asked me how to write to the board. I told her.

morning23.text: Three things. Answer what they ask. Say 'I don't know' when you don't. And don't mention the robot.

choose.text: Ready as I'll ever be.

then.text: That's what everyone says. Go on.

choose.text: I've held a bleeding spleen with steadier hands.

then.text: Good. Nervous people prepare.
then.head: nod

review_hod.text: Nirmala Rajan, chair of the board. Twenty years a judge, so I can tell a rehearsed answer. Don't bother.
Dr. Sethi gave us a very good presentation. Forty slides. Two about parking.
First question. A surgeon in your department makes a serious mistake, and asks you to keep it quiet. What do you do?

then.text: Before you answer. I have a pathology report that says 'retained surgical swab'. And a discharge letter that says 'adhesions'. Both about Mrs. Shanta Kurup. Both with your name on.

choose.text: I wrote 'adhesions'. Dr. Rao asked, and I agreed. It was wrong, and I'm sorry.

then.text: And I asked. Write that down too, Nirmala.
then.head: down

then.text: It's written.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Dr. Rao asked me to. He's my head of department.

then.text: I did. And a good surgeon says no to the head of department when the head is wrong.
Mrs. Kurup has written to us. She says you nearly didn't tell her, and then you did. She'd like both halves on the record.

choose.text: Both halves are true. I nearly didn't. I won't nearly not again.

then.text: Clumsy grammar. Honest answer. I'll take it.
then.head: nod

choose.text: We tell the patient, face to face, the same week. I learnt that by nearly not doing it.

then.text: The best rules are the ones we learn the hard way.
then.head: nod

else.text: Mrs. Kurup has written to us. Four pages. Mostly about a moustache. One line about you: 'The young surgeon made sure I was told the truth, to my face.'

choose.text: We tell the patient, face to face, the same week. Then we fix what let it happen. Then we look after the surgeon, because they'll carry it.

then.text: In that order?
then.head: tilt

then.text: In that order.

choose.text: Report it, investigate it, follow the policy. Every time.

then.text: Policies don't hold anyone's hand. Noted, though.

review_hod.text: Practical matters. The nurses' union wants a pay review, and two more nurses on every shift. The board has said no. As Head of Department, whose side are you on?

choose.text: The nurses'. Yesterday Priya ran an ambulance bay and sat with the dying. We can afford two more of her.

then.text: We can't, actually. But you'll find that out.

choose.text: Neither, yet. I'll sit down with both and find the money we're pretending we don't have.

then.text: Pretending. I'll pretend I didn't hear that.

choose.text: The board's. A department lives within its budget.

then.text: Say that to Grace before you say it to anyone else.

review_hod.text: Last question. Mine. What do you change on Monday?
review_hod.head: tilt

choose.text: The count rule goes on every theatre wall, and we check it's kept in a month.

then.text: My mistake, made into a rule. A better retirement present than the clock they're giving me.
then.head: nod

choose.text: Every junior operates with a senior's hands in their pockets, not over theirs.

then.text: Meera Iyer will be unbearable. She taught you that.

choose.text: Nobody is ever alone at night again. Not a doctor, not a nurse.

then.text: There goes another brochure.

review_hod.text: We've talked. Dr. Sethi is a fine surgeon. He'll be a fine head of something, one day.

then.text: It was close. Two votes to one. Mine was the one against.

review_hod.text: Head of Department, Surgery, {called}. From the first of the month.
My office. The door sticks; kick it on the left. And keep it open.
Your first budget meeting is Monday at eight. I've brought a brochure.
